NOW

Where the project stands

one new result

This card is the current state. The older summary below it is kept as a record and is marked where it no longer holds. Details, tables and every caveat are in section P2.

Established

  • On directed graphs the Rician closure is wrong and the dynamic theory is right. The shift of the synchronised branch, c = k (R − R0), pooled over 3 connectivities and 12 runs at p = 1, is -0.270 ± 0.009. The dynamic theory predicts -0.266 with no free parameter (0.5 standard errors away). The closure predicts -0.425 (17 standard errors away).
  • Two independent sets of fold runs agree. The cloud runs and the local runs used different seeds, sizes and relaxation times. Their fold coefficients differ by at most 0.6 combined standard errors across 4 comparable cells.
  • The stored summary is faithful to the raw runs. Recomputing every cell of the branch table from the run file reproduces the stored table to 4e-05.

Not established

  • The reaction (echo) term on undirected graphs. The branch shift at N = 20000 reads -1.00 at k = 12, -0.79 at k = 24, -0.68 at k = 48, -0.66 at k = 96, -0.78 at k = 192. It approaches the predicted -0.67 near k = 48 to 96 and then moves away again, and every one of those cells has only 2 seeds.
  • The fold coefficient on directed graphs. The closure is excluded, but 7 of 7 measured cells at p = 1 lie below the dynamic theory's 0.54. The leading-order number is too high at the connectivities reached.
  • Novelty of the mechanisms. They are not new: sparse dynamical mean-field and cavity frameworks (Metz 2025; Metz and Pérez Castillo 2026) and the symmetric-against-asymmetric comparison (Aonishi, Kurata and Okada 2002) already contain them. What appears new is the explicit coefficients for the adaptive model and their tests (docs/PRIOR_ART.md).
  • Everything that depended on the closure: the critical connectivity kc(p) and the effective connectivity for clustered graphs.
  • Any usable crash warning from synchrony (section B1): unchanged, still not detected.

Earlier summary (kept as a record)

Under audit. This summary was written before the audit in section P0. Items 1, 3 (the "12%" sentence) and 4 in the left column, and the false-alarm counts in the right column, are not currently supported by committed data. They are left in place so the record stays readable, and each is marked. Read section P0 for the measured values.

What holds up

  1. [Unverified, see P0] The finite-connectivity law for the fold (S14). Treating the local order parameter as a Rician variable rather than replacing it by R gives λb(p, ⟨k⟩) = γ(p+2)((p+2)/p)p/2 [1 + (p+2)/2⟨k⟩]. The bracket is new, has no free parameter, and its coefficient (p+2)/2 is exact both symbolically and numerically. It predicts the measured fold to 0.05% at ⟨k⟩ = 48 and to 0.6-3.7% at ⟨k⟩ = 12, and it accounts for the ~10% offset S11 and S13 could only report. The same closure gives a second threshold that exists only at finite connectivity, hence a critical connectivity kc(p) below which bistability is impossible at any coupling, and it absorbs clustering into a single effective connectivity keff = k/(1+(k−1)ρ).
  2. S13's two "new" results did not survive, and the correction is recorded (S13, S14). The threshold family is Zou & Wang, PRE 102, 012219 (2020) with α = p+1: their stability bound r² ≥ (α−1)/(α+1) is R*(p)². The p = 2 corner is Skardal & Arenas, Commun. Phys. 3 (2020), whose PDF was already in this repository. S13's own measurement could not have supported the claim either: its coupling grid quantised the reported ratio in steps of 4.09%, so the "flatness" of 0.055 was 1.3 grid steps wide. C* ≈ 0.35 was confounded by the same fixed grid no longer containing the transition above C ≈ 0.5. What survives is the qualitative claim, now derived in S14 instead of measured.
  3. Exact thresholds (S11). For Lorentzian frequencies the herding model is solvable in closed form: the cubic λR³ − λR + 2γ = 0 folds at R* = 1/√3, giving λb = 3√3 γ. The residual 12% against simulation is the finite-connectivity correction, which explains the ~10% offset S2 could only measure.
  4. [Not supported as stated, see P0] The first-order jump is genuine (S11). It grows with system size, 0.183 at N = 125 to 0.486 at N = 4000, rather than decaying. Not a finite-size artifact.
  5. What actually causes explosiveness (S8c). Not a frequency-degree rank correlation: with a Gaussian frequency law there is no jump at any correlation. The tail of g(ω) must match the tail of P(k), and even c = 0.75 gives almost nothing.
  6. Separability classification (A1). Kuramoto couplings are provably non-factorizable (D₁ ≡ 1, rank 2) and the herding coupling is an exact 3-body interaction, so the Hens et al. propagation theory does not cover them.
  7. Two model extensions earn their place (S10). State-dependent liquidity is the only change that produces fat tails or volatility clustering at all; inertia widens the bistable window 3.6x.

What did not hold up

  • The model's own network is wrong, but by less than was claimed (E5, corrected). The bistable window does collapse on networks estimated from real returns, and S4 and S5 both depend on that window, so the direction of the result stands. But the magnitude was overstated: an n-matched control, which E5 originally listed as an untested caveat, shows that a random graph at the real networks' own size already drops the gap from 0.793 to 0.396. 72% of the reported collapse was finite size, not clustering; the structural effect is a further 40% on top. Reading C against a size-matched baseline ⟨k⟩/n rather than against a single n = 400 graph, the real excess clustering is 3.8x, not 24x. S14 explains why the two effects are the same effect: in a small random graph neighbourhoods overlap by necessity, so keff falls for the same reason clustering lowers it.
  • [Direction kept, E8 counts withdrawn, see P0] No early warning, at any timescale, and it is not usable (E1, E7, E8). On daily data no indicator beats ordinary peaks. At 1-minute resolution over 2.3M bars the raw AUC is 0.911, but volatility-matched it is 0.526 [0.340, 0.712]. Out of sample co-movement needs 77.6 false alarms per crash caught; plain volatility is the better detector (65.2 at the same 1% budget) and co-movement with volatility removed is the worst of the three (274.5). The timescale objection is answered and E1 survives it.
  • λ cannot be measured (A3). Req(λ) is a step function, so 97.2% of market-days carry no information about λ, and a monotone transform cannot beat its own indicator. The headline recommendation is withdrawn.
  • Prior work does not fully generalize (E3). Lee et al. (PNAS 2025) does not reproduce at constituent level for 2008; out of sample across 262 events only the recovery half survives, weakly (ρ = 0.13).
  • Two proposed extensions must be rejected (S10). Contrarians destroy the transition entirely; asymmetric herding gives the wrong sign on the leverage effect.
  • No co-movement hysteresis in real data (E2), though S9 shows the test lacked the power to see the model's own prediction by a factor of four.
  • The repository's original degree-normalized model has no explosive synchronization (S1).

Status when this summary was written: the analytic core is in better shape than when this started (closed-form thresholds, a genuine discontinuity, a sharper cause), while the empirical case is weaker (no early warning at any resolution, and the central bistability largely absent on real networks). The most valuable next step is deciding whether E5's collapse is the clustering gap or an artifact of how the network was built, because steps S4 and S5 stand or fall on it.

Audit: which headline claims are actually backed by the files in this repository

audit in progress

This section was added after an external audit of the repository at commit fc98f02. It does two things. First, it re-runs the audit's three spot checks with this repository's own, unmodified functions (p0_spot_checks.py, output in data/p0_spot_checks.json). Second, it lists every headline claim next to the evidence that is really committed. Every number in this section is read from a result file when the page is built. No manuscripts are being written at this stage: nothing below is settled enough for that.

How to read the three tables

The quantity under test is the fold λb: the smallest coupling at which the synchronised state can still exist. All tables report it as a ratio to the exact all-to-all value γ(p+2)((p+2)/p)p/2 of Zou and Wang (2020), so a ratio of 1.000 means "no finite-connectivity effect" and a ratio of 1.125 means "the fold sits 12.5% higher than all-to-all". The Rician closure of S14 predicts the ratio 1 + (p+2)/(2⟨k⟩) at leading order.

Table A. Is the formula the correct expansion of the closure? Yes

Each cell is ⟨k⟩ × (closure ratio − 1). If equation (4) is the right expansion, the cells must approach (p+2)/2 as ⟨k⟩ grows. They do, to four digits. This confirms the algebra. It says nothing about whether the closure describes the network.

Table B. Is the measuring tool itself biased? No

The same bisection procedure (start fully synchronised, ask whether the synchronised state survives, halve the coupling interval), run on the exact all-to-all model with the same frequencies and the same survival threshold. It returns the known answer to within the bisection tolerance of 0.2% at every size. So when the tool disagrees with the closure on a sparse graph, the cause is the graph, not the frequency sampling and not the tool.

  • 8 of 10 values agree with the audit's table to within 0.1%. The largest difference is 0.38% (the run at ⟨k⟩ = 12, p = 1, relaxation time 480: 1.0574 here against 1.0533 in the audit). That is larger than the bisection tolerance of 0.2% and is most likely the chaotic sensitivity of a long run to the numerical library version, but it is far smaller than the gap to the closure, so no conclusion changes.
  • Simulation is below the closure in every row. The measured correction is 43% to 90% of the predicted one.
  • It is not slow relaxation. Raising the relaxation time from 120 to 480 on the same graph at ⟨k⟩ = 12 moves the ratio from 1.0513 to 1.0574, still far from the closure's 1.1184.
  • The spread between seeds is large and does not obviously shrink with N: at ⟨k⟩ = 12, p = 1 the 5 runs span 1.051 to 1.100 with mean 1.072. These are spot checks, not an ensemble, so no confidence interval is quoted. The fold of a sparse deterministic network appears to depend on the particular graph and the particular placement of frequencies on it.
  • New observation from this re-run, not in the audit. At ⟨k⟩ = 12 the surviving state just above the measured fold has R between 0.33 and 0.39, well below the closure's fold amplitude of 0.55 and close to the survival threshold of 0.55 R*. With the longer relaxation time it is 0.46. So part of what is being measured near the fold may be a slowly decaying or only partly synchronised state. The fold estimator's sensitivity to the survival threshold and to the relaxation time has to be mapped before any coefficient is quoted.
  • Most likely physical cause of the gap (a hypothesis, not a result): the closure treats the neighbours of node i as independent of node i. On a sparse graph each neighbour is itself pulled by node i, a back-reaction that a cavity (message-passing) calculation would include and the closure does not.

What has been done, and what happens next

  1. Done (phase 0). Spot checks reproduced; repository inventory, model specification and this claims audit written to docs/. No existing simulation code was changed.
  2. Next (phase 1). Move the simulator into a tested package with a regression test that it reproduces model.py exactly, so that no historical number can change silently.
  3. Phase 2. Fix the known defects: three different Lorentzian samplers, hidden run-order dependencies, the E7 overnight-gap contamination, the E8 look-ahead and scoring bugs, the E3 missing band-pass step, hand-typed numbers on this page.
  4. Phase 3. A systematic prior-art search before any novelty claim.
  5. Phase 4. The deciding measurement: random regular graphs, ⟨k⟩ from 6 to 96, four values of p, N up to 30,000, 5 seeds first and then 30, with the fold extrapolated to infinite size and a cavity theory compared against it. This needs cluster or GPU time.
  6. On hold by decision of the author. Manuscripts. They wait until phase 4 says what is true.
P1

New measurements and a leading-order theory of the fold at finite connectivity

pilot, not final

Incomplete pilot. The undirected pilot was interrupted before completion: 38 of 210 planned runs finished, all at N = 10000. The smaller sizes were never run, so there is no finite-size extrapolation. The directed-graph experiment was run separately and is complete.

This section reports what was measured after the audit, with a new compiled simulator that reproduces the old one to machine precision (56 regression and analytic tests). All numbers are read from results/ at build time. Runs: results/paperA_A1_pilot/20261013-015406_1e63e2d (interrupted before completion, partial), results/paperA_A7/20261013-175112_d49a0da-dirty, results/paperA_theory/20261013-024612_135bc4c-dirty. Derivation of the theory: docs/THEORY.md.

The idea in plain words

Each oscillator feels the average of its k neighbours. That average is the global synchrony R plus a scatter of size 1/√k. The Rician closure of S14 treats that scatter as frozen and as independent of the oscillator itself. Neither is right:

  • Part of the scatter rotates. Neighbours that are not locked keep rotating, so their contribution is an oscillating push, and an oscillator cannot follow a push that changes faster than its own relaxation rate. Only the frozen share, plus the slow part of the rotating share, acts. This lowers the correction.
  • The oscillator influences its own neighbours. On an undirected graph each neighbour is pulled slightly toward the oscillator, and the k slightly-pulled neighbours add up to an echo of the oscillator's own phase. The echo weakens the pull toward consensus. This raises the correction. It is absent on a directed graph, where neighbours do not listen back.

So the theory makes two predictions for the coefficient a(p) in fold = all-to-all fold × (1 + a(p)/k): one for directed graphs (first effect only) and one for undirected graphs (both effects). The Rician closure predicts the same value, (p+2)/2, for both.

Table P1.1. Predicted coefficients

Rician closure: all scatter frozen, no echo. Directed: rotating scatter filtered, no echo. Reaction term: the echo. Undirected: directed plus reaction. The last two columns split the variance of a neighbour's contribution at the all-to-all fold into the part that is frozen and the part that rotates.

Table P1.2b. The echo measured directly

Subtracting the directed coefficient from the undirected one at the same p, k and N isolates what two-way links add. Predicted echo is the reaction term of the theory evaluated at that k. The Rician closure predicts zero, because it gives the same coefficient to both kinds of graph. The uncertainty combines the two confidence intervals and treats the two sets of seeds as independent.

  • Undirected graphs: the 95% interval contains the new theory's value in 1 of 8 cells and the Rician value in 6 of 8. Directed graphs: the new theory in 3 of 4 cells, the Rician value in 0 of 4. Read the table, not this count, for the size of each discrepancy: both predictions are leading-order in 1/k and are expected to fail at small k.
  • The Phase 0 gap was mostly a size and relaxation-time effect. At k = 48, p = 1 the Phase 0 spot check (N = 1200, relaxation time 120, one seed) gave a ratio of 1.0233. The pilot (N = 10000, relaxation time 480, 5 seeds) gives 1.0292 [1.0254, 1.0330], against 1.0310 from the closure. The statement in section P0 that simulation sits below the closure in every run is true of those short, small runs and must not be read as a statement about the infinite-size fold.
  • The same contrast at the interactive demo's settings. With Gaussian frequencies, noise σ = 0.3, N = 500 and k = 12 (not the conditions the theory is derived for), the recovery threshold over 24 networks of each kind is 3.27 [3.24, 3.29] with two-way links and 2.98 [2.96, 3.00] with one-way links, a gap of 0.28 ± 0.02 (9.6%). The Rician closure cannot produce any gap, because it never asks whether links are mutual. Script: simulation/measure_echo.py; try it in block 10 of the simulation.
  • The fold varies from sample to sample. Mean standard deviation of the fold ratio across seeds on undirected graphs: N = 10000: 0.0066. Any single-seed fold is uncertain by about this much.
  • What is not established. Whether the coefficients converge to the predicted values needs larger k and N than this pilot. Nothing here tests the closure's critical connectivity or the clustering claim. The theory neglects loops, degree heterogeneity and second-order terms.

Why the test was moved off the fold

The fold is a poor place for a precision test. Its value differs from one network to the next by an amount that does not shrink quickly with N, the coefficient multiplies that scatter by k, and the expansion in 1/k is not analytic there (the next term is of relative order k−1/2). The same second-order expansion holds at every point of the stable synchronised branch, where none of this applies. Above the fold the self-consistency R = z0(λ Rp+1) + ⟨a2⟩/k gives a finite shift of the stationary synchrony:

k (R − R0) → c(λ) = ⟨a2⟩ / (1 − z0′(h) λ (p+1) R0p),   h = λ R0p+1

R0 is the synchrony of the all-to-all model at the same coupling, and ⟨a2⟩ is the second-order term of docs/THEORY.md section 3. The three treatments differ only in which neighbour scatter enters ⟨a2⟩: all of it (Rician closure), the frozen part plus the filtered rotating part (dynamic theory, directed graphs), or that plus the reaction term (undirected graphs). c is negative because finite connectivity lowers the synchrony of the branch.

Protocol. Coupling λ = 1.25 × the all-to-all fold. Start fully synchronised, relax for 150 time units, average R over the next 250. R0 is measured with the all-to-all kernel on the same frequencies at the same N, so the frequency clip and the finite frequency sample cancel in the difference. Measured references: p = 1, N = 20000: 0.77693; p = 1, N = 80000: 0.77686; p = 2, N = 20000: 0.85051.

Overlap k²/N is the expected number of nodes shared by the neighbourhoods of a node's neighbours; when it is not small, neighbour fields are correlated and the theory's independence assumption fails. Theory for this graph is the dynamic theory on directed graphs and the dynamic theory plus reaction on undirected graphs.

What the branch test shows

  • Directed graphs, p = 1: confirmed. The 3 cells with 4 seeds each (k = 12, 24, 48) pool to c = -0.270 ± 0.009. The dynamic theory's -0.266 is 0.5 standard errors away; the closure's -0.425 is 17 standard errors away. There is no fitted parameter, and the measured value does not drift with k.
  • Directed graphs, p = 2: compatible, weakly tested. Two seeds per cell. The point estimates sit on the dynamic theory, but the 95% intervals are too wide to count as a second confirmation.
  • Undirected graphs: suggestive, not confirmed. At N = 20000 the shift is -1.00 (k = 12), -0.79 (k = 24), -0.68 (k = 48), -0.66 (k = 96), -0.78 (k = 192) against a prediction of -0.67. It reaches the prediction only at k = 48 and 96 and departs again at k = 192. All of these cells have two seeds.
  • The k = 96 undirected point may agree by accident. Its overlap is 0.46. The directed run at the same k and N gave -0.13, and moved to -0.25 when N was raised to 80000 (overlap 0.12). So at N = 20000 a k = 96 point carries a finite-size error of that order, and the undirected point has not been repeated at larger N.
  • One coupling only. Every run is at 1.25 times the all-to-all fold. This is one point of the branch, not the curve c(λ).
  • The reference is shared. R0 is one all-to-all run per (p, N). Its error is common to every seed, is multiplied by k, and is not in the intervals. The two p = 1 references differ by 7.5e-05, which is 0.007 in c at k = 96 and 0.014 at k = 192: small, but not zero.

What the fold data add

  • Directed fold: the closure's value is excluded in every cell, by both sets of runs. The measured coefficient is below the dynamic theory's leading-order 0.54 in 7 of 7 cells at p = 1, so the leading-order number overestimates the fold shift at these connectivities.
  • Undirected fold: the Rician value is closer to the measurement than the new theory in 9 of 9 cells at p = 1. This is the cancellation described in section P1 (too much scatter, no echo), and it is the reason the closure looked right for so long.

Problems with the cloud run as a record

  • The runs were launched by hand, outside esfc run, so the directory has no env.txt or seeds.json. The settings in its config.yaml were written afterwards from the run note.
  • The last four lines of branch_runs.jsonl lack the timing and time-spread fields, so they came from an earlier version of the script.
  • 8 of 13 branch cells have two seeds and 2 have one. The widest two-seed interval spans 1.34 in c.
  • The run note states that no local config had results. That was out of date: the directed fold experiment is complete locally and the undirected pilot is partial (section P1).

Next steps, in order (revised after the external novelty audit)

  1. Reciprocity interpolation. Done at k = 24 and 48: section P3.
  2. Large connectivity with small overlap. k = 96 and 192, directed, half mutual and undirected, with k²/N at 0.05. Needs the cluster: configs/paperA_branch_ada.yaml.
  3. Tie the dynamic term to the exact directed theory. Show it is the leading 1/k expansion of the equation of Metz (2025), analytically or by population dynamics at small k.
  4. Derive the exponent of the non-analytic correction at the fold. Nodes about to unlock respond without limit, which should give a correction of relative order k−1/2. Derive it, then fit the fold data of table P2.2 with the exponent fixed and at least four connectivities.
  5. Branch curve. Several couplings and exponents (p = 1, 2, 3) on directed graphs with 10 or more seeds, against the three curves of table P3.1.
  6. Degree fluctuations. Erdős-Rényi graphs add their own 1/k term through the spread of degrees; measure it against random regular graphs.
  7. Forward threshold at finite k (a hypothesis, cheap to test): in the incoherent state the local order parameter is of order k−1/2, not zero, so incoherence may lose stability at a finite coupling that grows with k.
  8. Only then the critical connectivity and clustering, both derived from the closure.
P3

Reciprocity test: does the branch shift grow in proportion to the fraction of mutual links?

test of the reaction term

Section P2 left the reaction (echo) term unconfirmed, and an external novelty audit pointed out that the idea behind it is not new: comparing symmetric with asymmetric coupling to isolate an Onsager reaction term was done for oscillator networks by Aonishi, Kurata and Okada (2002), and the general sparse-graph frameworks of Metz (2025) and Metz and Pérez Castillo (2026) contain both mechanisms (docs/PRIOR_ART.md). What this project can add is a quantitative prediction and its test. This section is that test. Runs: results/paperA_reciprocity_gpu/20261024-230032_edf282f-dirty (on the GPU path, 10 seeds; the CPU run of 2026-10-14 was interrupted before writing rows), results/paperA_branch_theory/20261014-011900_be4f092-dirty. Configs: configs/paperA_reciprocity_gpu.yaml, configs/paperA_branch_theory.yaml.

The prediction

Take graphs in which every node listens to exactly k others, and make a fraction ρ of those links mutual (the node listened to also listens back) and the rest one-way. ρ = 0 is the directed graph of section P2 and ρ = 1 is an ordinary undirected random regular graph. The echo reaches a node only through neighbours that listen back, and there are ρk of them, so at leading order in 1/k:

c(ρ) = cdynamic + ρ × creaction

a straight line in ρ whose intercept and slope are both fixed by the theory. The Rician closure never asks whether links are mutual, so it predicts a horizontal line.

Table P3.1. Predicted branch shift, computed in this repository

The computed values differ from the copied ones by at most 4.6e-04, so the copied values were correct. R0 is the all-to-all synchrony at that coupling. Reaction is split into the part from locked nodes (closed form) and the part from drifting nodes (integrated numerically). All shifts are negative: finite connectivity lowers synchrony.

P5

Graph structure: clustering and degree heterogeneity

outside the leading-order theory

The theory assumes locally tree-like graphs with every degree equal (docs/THEORY.md section 5). This run measures how far each assumption matters at fixed mean degree: clustered random regular graphs with 0, 3 and 6 triangles per node (clustering about 0.005, 0.05 and 0.10 at k = 12) and Erdős-Rényi graphs. Run: results/paperA_structure_gpu/20261024-231842_edf282f-dirty. Config: configs/paperA_structure_gpu.yaml. The coefficient uses each graph's realised mean degree.

Reading

  • Clustering raises the fold modestly. At k = 12 the coefficient grows with the number of triangles at both exponents; at k = 24, where the same triangles give less clustering, the effect is within the intervals.
  • Degree heterogeneity lowers the fold strongly. With the 1/⟨k⟩ normalisation, high-degree nodes are coupled more strongly and hold the synchronised state. A heterogeneous mean field (Restrepo, Ott and Hunt 2005) is the natural extension of the theory.
  • Consistency. The random regular control agrees with the A1 pilot at the same k on independent seeds.
P6

Bistable window at low connectivity: is there a critical connectivity?

closure prediction tested

The closure predicts that below a critical connectivity the forward threshold (where a random, incoherent start synchronises) meets the fold, so bistability disappears (README: "unverified"). Both edges were measured on the same graphs and frequencies: the fold from a synchronised start (as in P1) and the forward threshold from a random start by the same bisection, waiting 400 time units per coupling. Run: results/paperA_window_gpu/20261025-003505_edf282f-dirty. Config: configs/paperA_window_gpu.yaml.

Reading

  • The window does not close where the closure says. At p = 1 the closure predicts a width below 0.007 for k ≤ 6; on undirected graphs the measured width there is 0.04 to 0.11 (95% interval above zero in 3 of 4 cells). At p = 2 the closure closes the window at k = 3 to 4 (predicted width -0.001 to 0.031); measured 0.09 to 0.15. Bistability survives down to k = 3.
  • Above it, the closure's width is close at p = 1: measured / predicted 0.90 to 1.06 for k ≥ 10, 1.57 at k = 8. At p = 2 the closure's width is too large at every k ≥ 8.
  • The width hardly depends on whether links are mutual. Directed and undirected widths differ by 6% (median, k ≥ 8), although both edges move a lot: at k = 3 the undirected fold is 2.52 times the all-to-all fold and the directed one 0.97 times.
  • On directed graphs at small k the fold lies below the all-to-all fold (p = 1: k ≤ 8, p = 2: k ≤ 4): the synchronised branch survives to weaker coupling than in the all-to-all model, opposite to every theory here (the closure predicts a fold well above it). The directed fold is therefore not monotonic in k: below 1 at small k, slightly above 1 near k = 12 to 24, and back to 1 as 1 + a/k at large k, which needs a large negative term of higher order in 1/k. A candidate is the floor of the local order parameter (about 0.89/√k for random phases), which keeps the herding gain large. It does not depend on N (p = 1, k = 4: 0.925 at N = 3000, 0.938 at N = 10000, 0.942 at N = 30000).
  • Reciprocity rescales the coupling. The undirected-to-directed ratio is the same for the fold and for the forward threshold: at p = 1 and k = 4 to 24 the two ratios differ by at most 2.3% (median 0.6%), while the ratio itself ranges from 1.04 to 1.64. Mutual links therefore act like a renormalised coupling, lambda divided by a factor f(k), which moves both edges of the window together and explains why its relative width hardly depends on reciprocity. At p = 2 the rule is approximate (up to 9.3%). At leading order f(k) = 1 + reaction / k.
  • Robust to N and to the waiting time. At N = 30000 the interval is above zero in 16 of 16 cells, and with the waiting time 1600 instead of 400 in 16 of 16. The window widens with N (undirected, p = 1, k = 4: 0.029 at N = 3000, 0.040 at N = 10000, 0.125 at N = 30000), so finite size narrows it rather than creating it: the widths at N = 10000 are lower bounds. The forward threshold is a first passage and depends on N; the width in the limit of large N is not yet fixed.

N1

Novelty audit: what is new, what is not, and what a referee will ask for

narrow but real

An external audit of the literature was run against the theory of section P1 (the summary is in docs/PRIOR_ART.md). Its conclusion changes how this work must be described, so it is given here in full. This section quotes no measured value of this repository; the measurements are in sections P1 to P3. The audit could not run full-text searches, so a paper with an explicit 1/k Kuramoto threshold could still exist in the literature it did not reach.

The conclusion in four sentences

  • The mechanisms are known. Filtering of fast neighbour fluctuations and the reaction of a node on its own neighbours are both contained in existing dynamical mean-field and cavity frameworks for sparse graphs.
  • The explicit results appear new. No published closed-form 1/k shift of the fold or of the synchronised branch was found for adaptive (local order parameter) Kuramoto oscillators on sparse graphs.
  • The right form is a regular article, framed as explicit leading-order sparse-graph corrections with a directed/undirected decomposition verified by simulation. It is not a new cavity method.
  • The finance study is kept separate. Attaching a weak empirical result to the physics would lead a referee to discount both.

Table N1.1. Prior work and how it relates

What it does describes the earlier paper. Overlap says which part of this project it anticipates. What to do is the action for the manuscript. Status records how far the description has been verified here: abstract checked means the arXiv abstract page was fetched and matches; from the audit means the description is the audit's and has not been checked against the paper; read earlier means it was read during the first search.

Hypothesis worth a cheap test

In the all-to-all model the incoherent state is linearly stable at every coupling, because the gain rp vanishes there. On a sparse graph the local order parameter of an incoherent state is of order k−1/2, not zero, so the effective coupling is finite. This suggests a finite forward threshold that grows with k, roughly as kp/2, which would make the width of the hysteresis loop finite and dependent on connectivity. This is the audit's inference, not a published result.

The finance study after the audit

  • The one positive number is exploratory. It comes from a robustness variant after the primary test did not reject, and must be reported that way.
  • A disjoint set of stocks is not an independent test. Crash events are market-wide and stock co-movement is dominated by a common factor, so different stocks over the same period test the same events. A confirmatory test needs a later time period with the event rule, horizon and volatility matching fixed in advance.
  • Benchmarks to include: the co-jump synchronization measures of Calcagnile et al. (2018) and the absorption ratio of Kritzman et al. (2011). Demirer, Leggio and Lien (2019) found no herding before the 2010 flash crash at one-minute resolution, consistent with co-movement being coincident and not leading.
B1

Corrected test of synchronization-based crash warnings on minute data, design fixed in advance

real data

This replaces E7 and E8. The design was written (docs/PREREGISTRATION_B.md) before this analysis was run, but it is not under version control, so that ordering rests on the author's word and on file times. It is also not a blind pre-registration: the earlier, flawed versions had been seen. Run: results/paperB_intraday/20261013-022708_20fb569. Data: 23 US large-cap stocks, 2,319,682 one-minute bars, 5,972 trading sessions, 2002-12-30 to 2026-09-24. Thresholds and the volatility regression are fitted on data before 2016 and applied unchanged afterwards.

What was wrong before, and what changed

  • Overnight gaps. Returns and 30-minute windows used to run across the overnight gap, so the open looked like a burst of co-movement. Now the first return of every session is dropped, the index restarts at each open, and no window crosses an open. Of the 31 onsets the old E7 detected, 6 were before 10:00.
  • Look-ahead. The regression that removes volatility from co-movement used to be fitted on the whole sample, test period included. It is now fitted on the training period only.
  • Alarm scoring. The old rule kept only the first alarm of each 390-minute stretch, so an alarm that had been on for more than an hour before a crash could never count. Now the alarm is a state per minute; a crash is caught if the state is on at any time in the 60 minutes before it; a false alarm is an episode with no crash within 60 minutes after it.

Table B1.1. Can the indicator tell a crash onset from an ordinary peak?

A crash onset is a local high followed by a fall of at least 3% within 60 minutes of the same session, at least 30 minutes after the open: 35 in total (23 before 2016, 12 after). AUC is the probability that a random crash scores higher than a random ordinary peak (0.5 means no skill). "Volatility-matched" pairs each crash with an ordinary peak of nearly the same volatility (25 pairs), so that an indicator cannot score merely by tracking volatility. Before a crash, volatility is 4.5 times its level before an ordinary peak.

Symbols and terms

θi(t)phase of trader/strategy i: position in its buy-sell cycle
qi = sin θinet order flow of i (+ buy, − sell); Q = ⟨qi⟩ is aggregate imbalance and moves the price
ωinatural frequency: how fast i cycles on its own (its trading horizon); spread Δω = strategy diversity
Aij, ki = Sinetwork (who observes whom) and degree of node i
λherding / coupling strength: how strongly traders copy observed order flow
ri = |ΣjAijeiθj|/kilocal agreement among i's neighbours (0 = split, 1 = unanimous)
ffraction of consensus-sensitive (herding) traders whose coupling is multiplied by ri
R = |⟨eiθ⟩|global synchrony (Kuramoto order parameter); crash = R jumps to ≈1 with Q ≈ −1
λf, λbforward (crash onset) and backward (recovery) thresholds; λb < λ < λf is the bistable window
σnoise intensity (idiosyncratic news)
τ, τ*trading-halt duration and minimum safe halt predicted by theory
τi ~ Siθlocal response time of node i to a neighbour's perturbation and its degree exponent (Hens et al. 2019)
AUCprobability that a random crash scores higher than a random non-crash (0.5 = no skill)
Kendall τ (trend)rank correlation of an indicator with time over the year before a date
S1

Explosive synchronization (Gómez-Gardeñes et al., PRL 2011)

reproduction

Question

Does the simulator reproduce the original explosive (first-order, hysteretic) transition, and does the repository's earlier degree-normalized model show it?

Setup

N = 1000, ⟨k⟩ = 6, ωi = ki (frequency-degree correlation), two networks per case, adiabatic sweeps (each coupling starts from the previous final state, 20 + 20 time units), Heun integrator dt = 0.004.

Script: s1_reproduce_gg2011.py

Model / derivation

Results

  • BA, unnormalized: forward jump at λf ≈ 1.56, backward at λb ≈ 1.31, max hysteresis gap 0.79.
  • ER control: continuous transition, gap 0.02, matching the paper.
  • Repo variant (K/ki): continuous, gap 0.06. Degree normalization destroys explosive synchronization, so the repository README's explosive-sync claim does not hold for that code.
S2

Herding feedback makes the market transition explosive (Zhang et al., PRL 2015)

reproduction

Question

If a fraction f of traders copy neighbours more strongly when those neighbours already agree, does the transition become explosive, and where is the bistable window?

Setup

N = 500, ⟨k⟩ = 12, Gaussian ω (σω = 1), f ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}, noise σ ∈ {0, 0.3}, 3 networks each, λ ∈ [0, 6] in 49 steps.

Script: s2_herding_explosive.py

Model / derivation

Mean-field (ER, f = 1): , so with and ; the minimum of λ(u) is λb.

Results

  • ER: the window opens only for f ≥ 0.75; at f = 1, λ ∈ [3.04, 3.88] (σ = 0) and [3.21, 3.96] (σ = 0.3).
  • Scale-free BA has a much narrower window (0.17 vs 0.83 at f = 1): heterogeneous networks resist herding-induced bistability, the opposite of the frequency-degree mechanism in S1.
  • Mean-field λb = 2.75 vs simulated 3.04 (≈10% low; the annealed approximation ignores finite-degree fluctuations of ri).
S3

Anatomy of a crash: flash, persistent and endogenous

mechanism

Question

Trader by trader, how does a crash unfold in the herding model, and which observable 'herding thermometers' react?

Setup

ER N = 500, f = 1, σ = 0.3, identical network, traders and noise in all scenarios. A: λ below λb plus a sell shock (ε = 1.2 for 8 time units); B: λ inside the window plus the same shock; C: λ ramped slowly past λf, no shock. All share a weak bearish news term (ε = 0.02).

Script: s3_crash_anatomy.py

Model / derivation

Results

  • A: synchrony spike, −7.6% V-shaped flash crash, full recovery once the shock ends.
  • B: the same shock locks the market into selling: −16.2%, price stays at 87 (hysteresis).
  • C: no shock needed: −19.2%; bursts of partial synchrony (flicker) precede the jump.
  • Without any directional news the locked herd's common phase drifts from selling to buying (boom-bust whipsaw), which is why the news term is included.
S4

Crash-type phase diagram and shock targeting

new result

Question

For herding λ and shock size ε, is a shock absorbed, a flash crash, or a lasting crash? Does it matter which traders are hit?

Setup

ER N = 500, f = 1, σ = 0.3. Grid 20 λ × 16 ε × 4 seeds (settle 60, shock 8, relax 150). Targeting: λ = 3.51, ε = 2, shock applied to a fraction φ of traders chosen by degree, natural frequency, or at random; 10 fractions × 5 strategies × 12 seeds.

Script: s4_crash_phase_diagram.py

Model / derivation

Classes: absorbed (R never exceeds 0.5), flash (exceeds 0.5 but relaxes), persistent (R ≥ 0.5 at the end), already crashed (R ≥ 0.5 before the shock).

Results

  • The flash/persistent boundary lies between λ = 3.1 (no lasting crash for any ε) and λ = 3.4 (lasting crash in every run for ε ≥ 0.23), bracketing λb = 3.21 from S2; above the smallest shock it does not depend on ε.
  • Inside the window the second-smallest shock (ε = 0.23) already gives a lasting crash; with the smallest (ε = 0.1) the probability climbs from 0 at λ = 3.4 to 1 at λ = 3.8.
  • From λ = 3.8 some markets crash before any shock (25% of runs), rising to 100% at λ = 4.3 (noise-induced escape near λf = 3.96).
  • Hitting 10-15% of traders is enough. At φ = 0.10 the probability of a persistent crash is 0.83 (hubs), 0.67 (random), 0.50 (slow traders), 0.17 (fast traders), 0.08 (periphery); at φ = 0.15 it is 1.00 for hubs, random and slow traders, 0.67 fast, 0.58 periphery. Hubs are the most and the periphery the least dangerous target; hubs vs random is within noise (12 seeds, SE ≈ 0.14), hubs vs periphery is not.
S5

Circuit breakers as desynchronization control

partly confirmed

Question

How long must a trading halt be to stop a locked-in crash, and which trigger works better?

Setup

Halt = coupling set to 0 (nobody sees anyone's trades) for τ; phases dephase at their own frequencies. (a) 8 λ × 16 τ × 8 seeds from a locked crash; (b) full price paths, 30 seeds, drawdown-7% vs breadth-triggered breakers, up to 4 halts; (c) partial halts.

Script: s5_circuit_breakers.py + theory.py

Model / derivation

During a halt from the locked state (locked phases ): Reduced criterion: trading resumes safely iff (the unstable branch = basin boundary), giving . Because and the dephasing time , .

Results

  • Theory reproduces the trend and order of magnitude but lies 16-44% below the simulated 50% boundary (theory/simulation = 0.56-0.84): 0.28 vs 0.49 at λ/λb = 1.02, 0.47 vs 0.68 at 1.06, 0.57 vs 0.68 at 1.10, 0.65 vs 0.93 at 1.15, 0.73 vs 0.93 at 1.19. The simulated boundary is resolved only to the τ-grid step (factor 1.38). (Corrects an earlier claim of close agreement.)
  • Halts lose effectiveness close to λf: the lowest re-crash probability over all τ ≤ 12 is 0 up to λ/λb = 1.10, 0.12-0.25 at 1.15-1.19, and 0.75-1.00 from 1.24 (λ ≥ λf), where noise re-triggers the crash.
  • Drawdown-7% breaker: τ = 0.5 re-fires (1.97 halts on average) and the market is still crashed in 97% of runs; τ = 1: 10%; τ = 2 and 4: 0%; τ = 8: 3%. Max drawdown falls from 16.0% without a breaker to 7.3-8.2%.
  • Breadth-triggered breaker (|mean sign of 10-period returns| > 0.6): max drawdown 4.1-4.6% for τ ≥ 1 (still crashed in 0-10% of runs), at the cost of more halts (1.1-4.0).
  • Partial halts (τ = 6): halting 20% of traders gives recovery probability 1.00 for every selection rule, as effective as a full halt (0.92-1.00). Hubs work with the fewest halted: at φ = 0.05 recovery is 0.58 (hubs) vs 0.00 (slow traders, random); at φ = 0.10 it is 0.92, 0.75 and 0.58.
S6

Early-warning signals in the model

negative result

Question

In the model, do classic early-warning signals fail before explosive transitions (as often claimed) while flickering works?

Setup

40 ramp/null pairs for explosive (f = 1, λ 2.0 → 4.6) and continuous (f = 0, λ 0.6 → 2.6) transitions; indicators on 100-unit windows up to 20 units before the jump; Kendall τ trend; ROC AUC ramp vs null.

Script: s6_early_warning.py

Results

  • No. var(R), AC1(R), index variance and AC1 all reach AUC ≈ 0.96-1.0 for both transition types.
  • Design limitation: nulls keep coupling fixed while ramps sweep it widely, so any indicator that grows with coupling scores well. This test cannot rank indicators.
  • Retracted: the earlier statement that flickering beats classic signals is not supported by the model.
S7

Does the speed of crowding matter? (rate-induced tipping)

negative result

Question

Does herding that builds up quickly crash the market when a slow build-up to the same level does not?

Setup

Herding ramps from λb − 0.8 to λhi inside the window over Tr ∈ [0.5, 500], then holds for 300 units; 4 levels × 7 ramp times × 24 seeds.

Script: s7_rate_tipping.py

Results

  • No rate effect: crash probability is flat in Tr within binomial error (±0.08).
  • It depends only on where λ ends: ≈0.2 at 30% into the window, ≈0.8 at 60%, ≈1.0 at 80-95%.
  • Inside the window the calm state is metastable: noise alone triggers crashes (e.g. 21% within 300 units at 30% depth).
A1

Is the model's differential equation separable? (Hens et al. framework)

analytic

Question

Hens et al. (Nat. Phys. 2019) predict how signals spread through networks, but only for dynamics of the form below with a product-separable interaction; they explicitly exclude G = M(xj − xi), i.e. Kuramoto. Where do our models stand?

Setup

Symbolic tests on each interaction G(x, y) (x = xi, y = xj), each confirmed numerically at random points. Hens' own models are included as controls.

Script: analytics/a1_separability.py (SymPy)

Model / derivation

Product separability: . Separable rank r (minimal number of product terms): the matrix is identically singular while the one is not. For Kuramoto : , hence so Kuramoto is never factorizable, but has rank 2. Difference kernels have finite rank iff M is an exponential polynomial (Levi-Civita), so has infinite rank. Herding input is not even additive: ; with it equals exactly , a 3-body (hypergraph) interaction. Exact herding Jacobian: (non-reciprocal, , rows sum to 0).

Results

  • Hens' SIS, regulatory and mutualistic models: product-separable (rank 1), D₁ = 0 as they must be.
  • Kuramoto, Sakaguchi, linear diffusive/Stuart-Landau: NOT product-separable (D₁ ≡ 1), separable rank exactly 2.
  • tanh diffusive: not separable at any finite rank.
  • Herding coupling: not pairwise-additive at all (cross-derivative up to 0.47); its ri² version is exactly a triadic hypergraph interaction.
  • Therefore Hens' theory does not apply to any of our phase models as published. This is the gap confirmed in Hens et al. 2019 (text excludes M(xj − xi), citing Kuramoto) and in Meena et al., Nat. Phys. 2023 (power/synchronization dynamics tested only numerically, “not covered by our analytical framework”).

Signal propagation beyond factorizable interactions: generalized theory and test

Question

Can Hens' degree-scaling law τi ~ Siθ be extended to non-factorizable (Kuramoto-type), infinite-rank, and non-additive (herding) interactions, with exponents predicted before simulation?

Setup

Scale-free (BA, m = 3) and ER (⟨k⟩ = 6) networks, N = 1000. Steady state by integration plus Newton (phase models in the co-rotating frame). A source node is clamped at x*j + δ; T(j → i) = time to half the final response (Hens protocol). τi = median T over sampled neighbours; θ = log-log slope with bootstrap CI. 160 sources per model/network; 4 per model re-run with the full nonlinear equations. Controls: Hens' SIS (θ = −1), regulatory a = 1 (θ = 0), a = 0.4 (θ = 3/2).

Script: analytics/a2_signal_propagation.py

Model / derivation

Generalization: for any neighbour-additive , configuration-model mean-field gives with , which is Hens' eq. (8) with . Hence Phase oscillators ( constant): ⇒ θ = −1 for = const and θ = 0 for . Herding: with ⇒ θ → −1 (crossover at ). Ratio interaction , (infinite separable rank): and (+1/3 for a = 0.5, −1/3 for a = 2), a value outside all Hens classes.

E1

Real data: do early-warning signals precede actual crashes?

negative result

Question

At a market peak, can any indicator tell whether a ≥10% crash (30% for crypto) follows within 30 trading days?

Setup

23 markets: US large/mid/small cap, UK 100/250, Germany, France, Spain, Switzerland, Netherlands, Italy, Sweden, Euro Stoxx 50, Japan, Hong Kong, India, Australia, Canada, Brazil, Korea, Singapore, 38 world indices (as nodes) and 40 cryptocurrencies; ≈2,900 constituents, daily 2000-2026 (current constituents: survivorship bias). Onset = true peak before the fall. Six indicators on 60-day windows using only past data. Three comparison sets; the fairest is peaks NOT followed by a crash. 95% CIs by cluster bootstrap over calendar quarters (a global crash hits many markets at once).

Script: empirical/e1_ews_all_markets.py (+ fetch_markets.py)

Model / derivation

Indicators on a trailing 60-day window (r = daily log return, i = stock, t = day): Scores at date d: level and trend = Kendall τ of the indicator against time over the preceding 250 days.

Results

  • 324 scored crash onsets in 23 markets, 69 distinct calendar quarters.
  • Against random dates several indicators look informative (AUC 0.59-0.63), but against ordinary peaks every indicator's 95% CI touches or includes 0.5: best AUC 0.571 (dispersion trend), variance level 0.567, flicker 0.547-0.552, correlation/absorption 0.52-0.54, lag-1 autocorrelation ≤ 0.52.
  • The event study shows why: all co-movement measures are flat until the peak and rise only after the fall begins. They react to crashes; they do not anticipate them.
  • Per-market AUCs (level score, ordinary-peak comparison) scatter from 0.31 to 0.71 with 8-22 scored crashes per market, consistent with noise over 23 × 6 = 138 tests.
  • Model-derived flicker is no better than plain variance.

E2

Real data: is there hysteresis in crashes?

negative result

Question

The model predicts crashes are bistable. Observable consequence: at the same volatility, co-movement should be higher on the way out of a crash than on the way in. Is it, beyond what ordinary volatility spikes show?

Setup

Same 23 markets. Daily 20-day volatility and co-movement. For each crash: pre branch [onset − 120, trough], post branch (trough, trough + 250]; volatility binned into 6 common bins; gap = mean post − mean pre co-movement. Placebo: high-volatility spikes ≥ 250 days from crashes. Positive control: the same real series with +0.03 added to co-movement after every trough.

Script: empirical/e2_hysteresis.py

Model / derivation

Results

  • 347 crashes, 62 placebo spikes, 23 markets.
  • Median gap 0.0006 (correlation), 0.0028 (absorption), 0.0031 (flicker), each with a 95% CI containing 0 (widest [−0.013, +0.014]); only 50-53% of crashes have a positive gap; crash vs placebo p = 0.53-0.77.
  • Positive control: a planted +0.03 is recovered as 0.031-0.033 with CI excluding 0, so the test has power, and any real co-movement hysteresis is smaller than ≈0.013.
  • Caveat: in the model's price mapping (S3b) return correlation does not track synchrony, so this rejects co-movement hysteresis in data but is not a direct refutation of the model's R-hysteresis.

S8

What actually makes the transition explosive

partly confirmed

Question

Topology, frequency law, frequency-degree correlation and noise are all said to drive explosive synchronization. Under one matched normalization, which of them really does?

Setup

Factorial sweep: 6 topologies (ER, BA, scale-free, Watts-Strogatz, ring, random regular) x 4 frequency laws x correlation c, all standardized to zero mean and unit scale so the coupling axis is comparable. N = 600, adiabatic sweeps. S8c repeats the correlation sweep after a design error was found in S8.

Script: s8_topology_frequency_sweep.py + s8c_correlation_corrected.py

Model / derivation

Correlation is imposed by a Gaussian copula, , which fixes the RANK correlation while forcing the marginal of . That is the error: the Gomez-Gardenes mechanism needs , i.e. proportionality, not ordering. With a Gaussian marginal the largest hub receives rather than .

Results

  • A Gaussian frequency law never produces a jump, at any correlation. ΔR stays flat at 0.08 from c = -1 to +1, with zero bistable window.
  • The jump appears only at |c| = 1 and only when the tail of g(ω) matches the tail of P(k): ΔR = 0.578 with a degree-matched marginal, 0.498 with a Lorentzian, 0.088 with a Gaussian. Even c = 0.75 gives almost nothing.
  • So the correct statement is not "frequency-degree correlation causes explosive synchronization", it is the tail of g(ω) must match the tail of P(k); a rank correlation is not sufficient.
  • No-free-parameter check against S1: predicted λf = 1.56·⟨k⟩/std(k) = 1.357, measured 1.562, ratio 1.15.
  • Noise erodes the transition monotonically but does not destroy it: ΔR 0.578 → 0.480 and the window 0.438 → 0.250 as σ goes 0 → 0.8.
  • Correction to S8 itself: the first factorial used too short a relaxation and returned negative hysteresis widths, which is unphysical. Only its ΔR values are quoted; S8c doubles the relaxation.
S9

The observable gap: why E2 could not have detected the model

new result

Question

E2 found no co-movement hysteresis and flagged a caveat about itself. Was that a refutation of the model, or a test without the power to see it?

Setup

The herding market with lambda ramped up through lambda_f and back down, co-movement measured with E1's own estimators, against real calm/crash levels from all 23 markets.

Script: s9_observable_mapping.py

Model / derivation

In S3's price map each asset is driven by its own order flow plus INDEPENDENT noise, so in a locked crash every is pinned and identically, at every . Adding one common market mode to the PHASE equation gives asset a loading on the shared shock, and with , the idiosyncratic variance, and in the weak-mode limit since . So .

Results

  • Real markets are unambiguous: co-movement rises from calm to crash in 23 markets out of 23, median +0.127 (0.229 → 0.389), from +0.029 (Brazil) to +0.265 (Japan). The unmodified model produces 0.000.
  • That zero is an identity, not a parameter choice: with independent per-asset noise the correlation is zero at every level of synchrony.
  • With the common mode on, crash co-movement rises 0.0001 → 0.0955 as σc goes 0 → 0.8, and the closed form ⟨u⟩² tracks it within about a factor of two.
  • The key number: E2's own gap statistic computed on the repaired model is 0.0002 to 0.0028 at every σc, against E2's detection bound of 0.013. Even with the mapping fixed the predicted effect is roughly four times smaller than the smallest one E2 could have seen.
  • So E2's null does not falsify the model's hysteresis. It is a negative result about the test, not the model.
  • But one channel is not enough: σc cannot produce a calm-period baseline (0.0006 against a real 0.229), while a common shock in the prices matches the level and produces no crash rise (+0.008 against +0.127). A calibrated model needs both.
S10

Do the proposed extensions actually improve the model?

partly confirmed

Question

Eighteen extensions were proposed. Which of them measurably move the model toward real markets, and which quietly destroy the phenomenon they were meant to explain?

Setup

Eight phase-side variants x four price mappings, scored against the 23 markets on excess kurtosis 10.20, volatility clustering 0.246, leverage effect -0.113 and crash co-movement 0.389. Lambda cycles across the bistable window so each run contains real crash episodes.

Script: s10_extensions.py

Results

  • State-dependent liquidity is the single most valuable addition. It appears in every top-scoring combination and is the only change that produces fat tails or volatility clustering at all: kurtosis 0.035 → 2.06, clustering 0.008 → 0.34. Without it the model's returns are Gaussian white noise.
  • Volatility clustering (target 0.246) and crash co-movement (target 0.389) are now reproduced. Fat tails improve 59-fold but remain 5x short of the real 10.2.
  • The leverage effect is not reproduced by anything. Asymmetric herding was added specifically for it and produces the wrong sign (+0.007 to +0.100 against a real -0.113) while halving the bistable window. Rejected.
  • Contrarians destroy the transition entirely. Just 15% of desks leaning against observed flow collapses the hysteresis gap to 0.108 from 0.767 and R never reaches 0.5. Rejected as an improvement, but it is a finding: market makers look structurally stabilizing.
  • Inertia widens the bistable window 3.6x (0.675 → 2.400), confirming that it supplies hysteresis independently of any frequency-degree correlation.
  • Keep: liquidity, common mode, inertia. Reject: contrarians, asymmetric herding.
  • Correction to this test: its first version held lambda fixed inside the window and measured frac_crashed = 0.0 for every variant, so the returns were pure noise and the whole comparison was vacuous. The cycling design replaced it.
E3

Real data: does Lee et al. (PNAS 2025) generalize?

negative result

Question

Lee et al. report that a market's pre-crisis proximity to explosive synchronization predicts how fast it collapses and recovers, validated on 39 country indices in the 2008 crisis. Does that hold at constituent level across 26 years?

Setup

Their estimator implemented exactly: Hilbert transform each stock's returns, build the instantaneous Kuramoto order parameter across the market, take the ACF of it in overlapping moving windows, and use the kurtosis of those ACF values as ES proximity. 315 events, 23 markets, cluster bootstrap over markets.

Script: empirical/e3_lee_reproduction.py

Results

  • The 2008 result does not reproduce at constituent level (n = 53): collapse ρ = -0.207 with CI [-0.435, +0.015], recovery ρ = -0.017. Neither is significant.
  • Out of sample across 262 other events, the recovery half survives: ρ = +0.133, CI [+0.038, +0.215], and the sign is the one hysteresis predicts (closer to explosive means a more prolonged recovery). The collapse half does not (ρ = +0.080, CI includes zero).
  • The surviving effect is weak: ρ = 0.13 explains under 2% of the variance.
  • Not an exact replication. They used 39 country indices from Compustat Global; this uses constituent-level Yahoo data inside 23 markets, so the networks differ and survivorship bias applies here.
E4

Real data: does the answer change intraday?

real data

Question

The model describes intraday synchronization but E1 and E2 tested daily closes, three orders of magnitude coarser. Is the null result just a timescale mismatch?

Setup

Hourly bars for 119 large US names, the deepest free history available (730 days). E1's event study repeated on that grid, with the same matched-peak null.

Script: empirical/e4_intraday.py

Results

  • Hard data limit: Yahoo serves 1-minute bars for 7 days, 5-minute for 60 days and hourly for 730 days, so the 2010, 2015 and 2018 events cannot be tested without a paid feed. Hourly is about a 7x improvement over daily, not the full fix.
  • At hourly resolution co-movement is elevated before crashes but not before ordinary peaks (0.206 against 0.123 sixty bars ahead), giving AUC 0.717 against E1's 0.542 on daily data.
  • But there are only 6 events. Observations inside one event are heavily autocorrelated, so the effective sample size is about 6, not 72. Event-level sign test: 5 of 6.
  • Suggestive, not significant. The value of this result is that it identifies a paid intraday feed, rather than more daily data, as the way to settle E1 and E2.
A3

Can the herding coupling be measured in a real market?

negative result

Question

Every operational claim here is phrased as where lambda sits relative to lambda_b, yet lambda has never been measured. Can it be recovered from observable co-movement?

Setup

Invert the S9 mapping to get R from measured co-movement, then invert the model's own equilibrium curve R_eq(lambda) to get lambda, for 27,723 market-days across 23 markets.

Script: a3_lambda_estimation.py

Model / derivation

Results

  • This does not work, and the reason is structural. Req(λ) is very nearly a step function, jumping from R = 0.137 to R = 0.899 across a λ window only 0.167 wide.
  • 97.2% of real market-days land inside that blind region, so the estimate has an inter-quartile range of 0.04. The discontinuity that makes explosive synchronization interesting is exactly what makes its control parameter unidentifiable from its order parameter.
  • Even a perfect inversion could not help. The estimate is a monotone transform of mean correlation, and AUC is invariant under monotone transforms, so it must score identically to the raw indicator. No reparametrization of an indicator can beat that indicator.
  • This kills what had been this repository's headline recommendation, and it is reported rather than dropped.
  • An earlier version of this script reported AUC 0.949. That was an artifact of a thinning bug leaving only 8 comparison points.
S11

Exact thresholds, and does the jump survive N to infinity?

analytic

Question

S2's mean field was numerical and about 10% off. Can the herding model be solved exactly for Lorentzian frequencies, and is the first-order jump real or a finite-size artifact?

Setup

Closed-form solution of the cubic for Lorentzian g, checked against a direct N = 2000 simulation; then a finite-size sweep from N = 125 to N = 4000, 3 seeds per size.

Script: s11_analytics.py

Model / derivation

The classic Kuramoto result , , has the mean field entering as . In the herding model the gain is , so it enters as , i.e. . Substituting gives a cubic whose fold (double root, ) sits at , and back-substitution gives the closed form

Results

  • Closed form for the recovery threshold: λb = 3√3 γ, with R* = 1/√3 at the fold. Verified: at λ = 5.2, just above the fold, the two roots are 0.5901 and 0.5645, converging on 0.5774 as they must.
  • Simulation at N = 2000 gives λb = 5.800 against the exact 5.196, ratio 1.116. That 12% gap is not an algebra error, it is the finite-connectivity correction: the closed form is exact for all-to-all coupling while the simulation runs on a sparse graph with ⟨k⟩ = 12. This explains the ~10% offset S2 could only measure.
  • Finite-size: the jump GROWS with N, 0.183 at N = 125 to 0.486 at N = 4000, and so do the hysteresis gap (0.119 to 0.473) and the window (0.000 to 0.400). A finite-size artifact would decay toward zero, so the first-order discontinuity is genuine and the values quoted elsewhere at N = 500 are if anything conservative.
  • Caveats: 3 seeds per size, the trend is not perfectly monotone (N = 2000 dips), and the window is resolved only to the 0.2-wide λ grid.
E5

Real data: the model on a REAL market network

negative result

Question

Every structural claim here rests on synthetic ER or BA graphs. What happens on a network estimated from actual market data?

Setup

Two networks per market from daily returns, thresholded to the same mean degree (12) as the synthetic benchmark so degree is fixed and only structure differs: correlation-thresholded, and lead-lag (i leads j at +1 day more than the reverse, then symmetrised). US, UK, Japan, Germany.

Script: empirical/e5_real_network.py

Results

  • Real market networks are an order of magnitude more clustered than anything used elsewhere here: C = 0.731 (correlation) and 0.138 (lead-lag) against 0.030 for synthetic ER and 0.081 for BA. κ is 1.80 to 1.98 against 1.09 for ER.
  • The bistable window essentially vanishes on them. Hysteresis gap 0.793 on synthetic ER falls to 0.172 (correlation) and 0.190 (lead-lag), and the window width goes to zero (-0.100 and 0.000 against 0.800).
  • This is the most serious result in the repository. S4 (crash persistence is set by the hysteresis branch) and S5 (minimum safe halt duration), the two most novel items, both depend entirely on that window existing. On a network estimated from real data there is no window for a shock to leave the market in.
  • Likely mechanism: the clustering gap. When neighbours share neighbours, local agreement ri saturates locally instead of propagating globally, which is exactly the positive feedback the herding route needs. It also means the annealed mean field, which assumes no clustering, does not apply to the real networks either.
  • Caveats, stated plainly: the real networks are smaller (n = 125 to 335 against 400) and the thresholding is a modelling choice, not an observable. Neither explains a fourfold collapse of the gap, but both should be checked at matched n and across thresholds before this is treated as settled.
E6

Real data: the 2010 flash crash at 1-minute resolution

real data

Question

The model is intraday and the 2010 flash crash lasted 36 minutes. Does co-movement rise BEFORE 14:32, which daily data said it does not?

Setup

1-minute bars for 32 large caps over 3-7 May 2010 (HF Data Library, CC BY 4.0, 2002 to present). Same co-movement estimator as E1 and the same order parameter as E3.

Script: empirical/e6_flash_crash.py

Results

  • Co-movement rose +0.137 in the 92 minutes BEFORE 14:32 (0.336 baseline to 0.473) and then fell slightly during the crash itself. On daily data E1 found the reverse: flat until the peak, rising only afterwards.
  • But the null cuts the claim down. Running the same 13:00-14:32 window on every day that week, the crash day has the largest afternoon rise (+0.141) but 2010-05-05 reaches +0.115, and the crash day's absolute level (0.473) is not even the week's highest (2010-05-07, the aftermath, at 0.623).
  • With one crash and four control days, inside a week already dominated by the European debt crisis, this cannot separate a genuine precursor from ordinary intraday variation.
  • Suggestive, not established. It motivates E7 rather than settling anything.
E7

Real data: the timescale objection, settled at 1-minute resolution

negative result

Question

E1 and E2 tested daily closes while the model describes intraday synchronization. Was the null result just a resolution artifact?

Setup

23 tickers, 2,319,682 one-minute bars from 2002-12-30 to 2026-09-24 (HF Data Library, CC BY 4.0). 31 intraday crash events (a 3% fall of the equal-weight index within 60 minutes) against E1's own matched null of local maxima not followed by a fall, one value per event so events rather than minutes are the unit.

Script: empirical/e7_minute_event_study.py

Results

  • The unmatched result looks spectacular. Pre-event co-movement is 0.458 before crashes against 0.228 before ordinary peaks, AUC 0.911 [0.843, 0.969], against E1's 0.542 on daily data. Taken at face value this says E1's null was a resolution artifact.
  • It is not. Crashes happen in high-volatility regimes and co-movement rises with volatility, so an unmatched comparison scores well purely as a volatility proxy. Pre-event volatility is 4.94x higher before crashes (0.00151 against 0.00031).
  • Pairing each crash with the nearest-volatility ordinary peak without replacement, exactly the control E1 used on daily data: AUC falls from 0.897 to 0.526, CI [0.340, 0.712], which spans chance. Median co-movement is 0.459 against 0.409 for matched peaks.
  • Once volatility is held fixed, co-movement carries no skill at minute resolution either. The same confound structure appears at both timescales.
  • This settles the single biggest threat to the empirical chapters. Assumption 41 held that the daily grid might be three orders of magnitude too coarse and that E1 and E2 could be measuring nothing but that mismatch. Tested at the model's own timescale across 24 years, E1's conclusion survives the test it was most vulnerable to. It also retires recommendation A15.
  • Caveats: 21 crashes survive the pre-window data requirement, so the matched interval is wide, and the cross-section is 23 large caps rather than a full index. A larger ticker set would tighten it, but 0.526 is not close to meaningful skill.
S12

The last three structural extensions

negative result

Question

Do a co-evolving network, a multilayer structure, or a bipartite trader-asset mapping improve the model?

Setup

Same protocol as S10: lambda cycles across the bistable window, scored on four stylised facts plus whether the window survives.

Script: s12_structural_extensions.py

Results

  • A11 co-evolving network: reject. Its one notable effect is counter-intuitive. Rewiring toward desks that already agree reduces global synchrony (R 0.926 to 0.712 at a 20% rewire rate), because homophily fragments the network into like-minded clusters. Local order, global disorder: an echo chamber, not an amplifier.
  • A12 multilayer: reject. Best stylised-fact score of the three, but it destroys the bistable window (gap 0.465 against 0.789, lambda_b undefined). Same verdict as contrarians in S10: it improves the fit by removing the phenomenon.
  • A13 bipartite trader-asset: no effect. Structurally it is the correct fix for assumption 29, but every stylised fact is slightly worse and crash co-movement is unchanged.
  • None of the three is worth adopting. With S10 that is five of eleven tested extensions rejected on evidence.
E8

Real data: could you actually have called a crash?

negative result

Question

E7 reported AUC, which ranks. Fix a threshold, make real calls out of sample, and count them: how many crashes are caught, and at what cost in false alarms?

Setup

Thresholds fixed on 2002-2015 at a set alarm budget, then applied unchanged to 2016-2026. 10 crashes across 2,697 test trading days, a base rate of 0.37%. Three detectors: raw co-movement, volatility alone, and co-movement after regressing out log-volatility.

Script: empirical/e8_prediction.py

Model / derivation

Co-movement regressed on log volatility has : 41% of co-movement is just volatility. The residual is the synchronization-specific component the model actually claims.

Results

  • Nothing is usable. The best detector catches half the crashes at 77.6 false alarms per catch, precision 0.0127 against a base rate of 0.0037. TP 5, FP 388, TN 2299, FN 5.
  • Volatility alone is the best of the three (precision 0.0151, 65.2 false alarms per catch). It beats the model's own observable.
  • Removing the confound makes it worse, not better. Co-movement with volatility regressed out is the worst detector: precision 0.0036, recall 0.20, 274.5 false alarms per catch, falling to 1173 at a 5% budget.
  • E7 showed the ranking signal was volatility. E8 shows that what remains after removing volatility is not merely weak but actively unhelpful, out of sample, at the model's own timescale.
  • This closes the empirical question. Across 23 markets daily, 730 days hourly, and 2.3M minute bars, there is no operationally useful crash precursor in co-movement.
S13

Two claimed new results, and what survived a literature check

claim withdrawn

Question

Everything else here reproduces known work or reports a negative result. Is there anything positive and new?

Setup

H1: generalise the herding gain to alpha_i = r_i^p, solve the fold exactly, and test against simulation at N = 1500 for p in {0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3}. H2: sweep Watts-Strogatz rewiring at fixed mean degree, which holds kappa at 1.00-1.04 and so isolates clustering from degree heterogeneity.

Script: s13_new_hypotheses.py

Model / derivation

With the mean field gives , and substituting into the exact Lorentzian result yields The fold, where , gives a closed form for every : One expression spans three separately studied models: gives (plain Kuramoto, continuous), gives (pairwise herding), and gives (the exact 3-body hypergraph interaction A1 identified).

Results

  • H1 is not new, and the claim is withdrawn. The family is Zou & Wang, Phys. Rev. E 102, 012219 (2020), who study exactly a mean-field force , i.e. . Their stability result reads, verbatim, that the locked states are stable "only for if . For , is predicted at the coupling threshold ." With , , which is — same formula, same symbol for the threshold, five years earlier.
  • The corner is separately exact in Skardal & Arenas, Commun. Phys. 3 (2020): their saddle-node curve gives at with . That PDF was already in this repository's own reference folder. The observation that coupling is a 3-body interaction is stated in one line by Xu et al., Phys. Rev. Research 3, 043004 (2021).
  • The nearest active work is the Hens group's own: Dutta et al., Phys. Rev. Research 7, L022049 (2025) and arXiv:2507.18421 (2025) run power-law adaptation of the order parameter with both an adaptation exponent and a partial-adaptation fraction , on hypergraphs, via Ott-Antonsen. That is this model, with this , analysed more generally.
  • The measurement could not have supported the claim either. H1's coupling grid was linspace(0.45·pred, 1.8·pred, 34), whose step is 4.09% of the prediction at every p. The 12 runs therefore produced only three distinct ratio values (1.0636, 1.1045, 1.1455), and the reported flatness of 0.055 is 1.3 grid steps wide. A drift of a few percent with p — which is exactly what S14 shows is really there — was invisible by construction. The quoted "1.105 ± 0.055" is also mislabelled: the standard deviation over the 12 points is 0.035, and 0.055 is the range of the four per-p means.
  • Separately, was read off as the grid point where the backward branch crosses , while the theory's own fold amplitude moves from 0.447 at to 0.707 at . At the fold sits below the detection level. The estimator's bias therefore varies with p across precisely the range where p-independence was being asserted.
  • H2's C* ≈ 0.35 was confounded by the coupling range. The sweep used a fixed grid linspace(2, 11, 31) at every clustering level, but rises with clustering: 5.9-6.5 at C=0.014, 6.8-7.7 at C=0.354, then 8.0/11.0/undefined at C=0.503, and undefined for all three seeds at C = 0.586, 0.641 and 0.682. Above C ≈ 0.5 the transition had left the scanned box, so the small gap there means only that both branches stayed incoherent. The single clustering level above C* with a measured transition is C = 0.354 itself.
  • What survives, and is now derived rather than measured. The qualitative claim that clustering closes the window holds, and S14 replaces the measured threshold with a predicted one by showing that clustering acts entirely through an effective connectivity. The prior art the original write-up cited for this (Chaos 33, 053103, 2023) turns out to be a different mechanism: it uses a degree-biased Laplacian on trees and Cayley graphs, and its result is about cycle length, with long cycles suppressing the transition strongly and triangles behaving erratically. So H2 was conceded too generously and H1 not nearly enough.
S14

A Rician closure for the local order parameter: the finite-connectivity law for the fold

unverified, under audit

Question

S11 and S13 both measured a fold about 10% above the all-to-all prediction (ratios 1.116 and 1.105 at ⟨k⟩ = 12) and had no explanation. That offset is the only thing in S13 the literature does not already contain. What is it?

Setup

Theory: keep the local order parameter r_i as a random variable instead of replacing it by R. Measurement: lambda_b by bisection on the survival of the upper branch, with NO coupling grid, on random regular graphs (every degree exactly k, so the theory applies with no degree heterogeneity), Erdos-Renyi graphs at the same mean degree, and Watts-Strogatz graphs at fixed ⟨k⟩ = 12. N = 2000, p in {0.5, 1, 1.5, 2}, ⟨k⟩ from 6 to 96, 5 seeds.

Script: s14_finite_connectivity.py

Model / derivation

The annealed mean field replaces by . But the exact locking field is and is the modulus of a sum of unit vectors. By the central limit theorem that sum is complex Gaussian with mean and total variance , so is a Rician variable with scale per component: a coherent part plus a scattered part, exactly as in Rician fading. The second ingredient is what makes the closure correct. Node does not lock to the global mean phase ; it locks to the direction of its own neighbour sum, which is itself random. Its contribution therefore carries a projection factor , and the self-consistency becomes with , , . Keeping the projection factor is essential: without it stops being a solution, because a sparse graph has even when incoherent, and the closure would predict ignition out of nothing. With it, is odd in at and the incoherent state is preserved exactly. Expanding to and shifting the fold gives the result: The factor appears twice. Linearising the same closure about gives a second threshold that does not exist all-to-all, with — the same that sets the incoherent floor. Finally, if the neighbours of are themselves linked their phases correlate, so the variance becomes and everything above holds with an effective connectivity Sparsity, clustering and small system size are then the same effect in different units.

Results

  • Audit status, read this first. The findings below describe the closure, which is an approximation. They are not yet confirmed as statements about the network model. An independent re-run of this script's own bisection (section P0) on random regular graphs at ⟨k⟩ = 12, p = 1 gives a fold ratio between 1.051 and 1.100 over 5 runs, against 1.118 from the closure and 1.125 from equation (4). Simulation sits below the closure in every run. At ⟨k⟩ = 48, p = 1 the re-run gives λb = 5.3171 against 5.3585 from equation (4), a difference of -0.77%, not the 0.05% quoted below. The measured values quoted in the findings below (the 0.05% agreement, the 0.6 to 3.7% range, the clustering table, and the five-seed error bars in the figure caption) come from a run whose output files were never committed, so they cannot be checked and are withdrawn until re-measured. The word 'exactly' applies to the closure only.
  • The coefficient is exactly . Numerically converges to 1.24935, 1.49982, 1.75005, 2.00021 at = 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 against = 1.25, 1.50, 1.75, 2.00. Symbolically the shift evaluates to exactly at = 1/4, 1/2, 1, 3/2, 2 and 3.
  • The closure's central assumption is testable on its own, and it holds. Simulating a locked state and comparing the observed spread of the neighbour sums against the predicted Rician scale gives a ratio of 1.215 at ⟨k⟩ = 6, 1.091 at 12, 0.998 at 24 and 0.919 at 48, and the predicted mean of matches the observed one to three decimals from ⟨k⟩ = 12 upward. A Kolmogorov-Smirnov test against the full Rice law passes at ⟨k⟩ = 48 (p = 0.30) and fails at small ⟨k⟩, which is the central limit theorem converging exactly as it should for a sum of k unit vectors.
  • It predicts the measured fold with no fitted parameter. At ⟨k⟩ = 48 on random regular graphs, equation (4) gives 5.3585 against a measured 5.3558 for (0.05%) and 8.3333 against 8.3291 for (0.05%). At ⟨k⟩ = 12 it gives 9.333 against 9.278 for (0.6%) and 5.846 against 5.632 for (3.7%), where the term is no longer negligible.
  • It explains why S13's ratio looked flat, and says it is not. The offset should grow with p as , from 10.4% at to 16.7% at when ⟨k⟩ = 12. The measured ratio does grow, 1.084 to 1.160 across that range. S13 could not see it because its grid quantised the ratio in steps of 4.09%.
  • A second threshold exists only at finite connectivity. All-to-all, the incoherent state is linearly stable for every coupling, which is why has always been reported as a fluctuation-driven, N-dependent quantity rather than a constant of the model. At finite ⟨k⟩ the residual floor gives it a genuine linear instability at a finite , and means this happens at all only for . Predicted at ⟨k⟩ = 12: 6.97 () and 19.76 (), against simulated of 5.74-5.95 and 13.4-14.1. The linear threshold is an upper bound and the sweep ignites below it, which is the expected direction.
  • Bistability needs a minimum number of neighbours. The window narrows as connectivity falls and closes at a critical : relative width 1.93 at ⟨k⟩ = 96 falling to 0.0027 at ⟨k⟩ = 6 for . decreases with p, so higher-order coupling makes bistability more robust to sparsity, not less.
  • Clustering is lost connectivity, and this is what replaces S13's C*. is read straight off the observed spread of the neighbour sums, with no free parameter and without estimating separately. The critical clustering is then not a measured threshold but the point where crosses .
  • The same formula explains E5's finite-size confound. For an Erdos-Renyi graph the neighbourhood overlap is , so a small random graph already has correlated neighbourhoods and a reduced . E5's rerun with n-matched controls confirms it: 72% of the reported collapse of the bistable window was finite size, not clustering.
